nameStory: This woodpecker gets its name from its brilliant crimson-red head that looks like it's been dipped in bright red paint. The scientific name 'erythrocephalus' literally means 'red head' in Greek, making this one of the most straightforward bird names you'll encounter!
description: The Red-headed Woodpecker is a mid-sized woodpecker with one of the most striking color patterns in North America. Adults have a completely bright red head and neck, contrasting sharply with their solid black back and wings, and clean white underparts. They're about the size of a Robin, with the typical woodpecker body shape - sturdy build, strong bill, and zygodactyl feet (two toes pointing forward, two back) for gripping tree bark.

idTips.label: Solid Red Head
idTips.description: The entire head and neck are brilliant crimson-red with no patterns or markings - like wearing a bright red hood that covers everything above the shoulders

idTips.label: Bold Color Blocks
idTips.description: Three distinct color blocks: solid red head, jet black back and wings, and bright white chest and belly with sharp, clean borders between colors

idTips.label: White Wing Patches
idTips.description: Large white patches on the wings become very obvious in flight, creating a striking black-and-white pattern against the sky

idTips.label: Smooth Black Back
idTips.description: The back appears solid black without the barred or striped patterns you see on most other woodpeckers - smooth as a bowling ball

idTips.label: Typical Woodpecker Call
idTips.description: Makes a harsh 'kweer-kweer' call and the familiar drumming sound on wood, though they're often quieter than other woodpeckers

habitat: Red-headed Woodpeckers prefer open woodlands, forest edges, parks, and areas with scattered large trees rather than dense forests. In New England, look for them in oak groves, along woodland borders near fields, in large cemetery parks with mature trees, and in areas where dead trees (snags) are left standing. They need open space for their unique hunting style of catching insects in flight.

seasonality.spring: Adults return to breeding areas and begin courtship displays. This is when their red heads are most vibrant and they're most active and vocal around potential nesting sites in dead trees.
seasonality.summer: Peak breeding season with adults feeding young. You might see them making dramatic flights from perches to catch flying insects, and hear frequent drumming on dead wood.
seasonality.fall: Adults and juveniles may be seen gathering and storing nuts and acorns for winter. Young birds still have brownish heads rather than the brilliant red of adults.
seasonality.winter: Less common in northern New England as many migrate south. Those that remain are often quieter and focus on cached food supplies, making them harder to spot.

funFact: Red-headed Woodpeckers are one of the few woodpecker species that regularly catch insects on the wing like flycatchers, making acrobatic flights from perches to snatch flying ants, beetles, and other insects right out of the air!
confusionNotes: Most commonly confused with the Red-bellied Woodpecker, but remember: Red-headed has a completely red head like a red cap, while Red-bellied has a black-and-white striped back and only a red cap on top of the head (despite its confusing name, the belly is barely pinkish). Memory trick: Red-headed means the WHOLE head is red, not just the top!
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'Red-bellied,' the Red-bellied Woodpecker actually has a red head too, which creates naming confusion. The Red-bellied was named for a subtle reddish wash on its belly that's barely noticeable, while the Red-headed was named for its obvious feature - proving that whoever named these birds had different priorities!
compareHints: Within the Melanerpes genus, Red-headed Woodpeckers are easily distinguished from their cousin the Red-bellied Woodpecker by their solid black backs versus the Red-bellied's distinctive black-and-white barred pattern. Red-headed also have completely red heads and necks, while Red-bellied have grayish faces with red only on the crown and nape.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Unlike its close relative the red-headed woodpecker, which has solid blocks of color (red head, black back, white belly), the red-bellied woodpecker shows a more complex pattern with its barred back and subtly colored underparts.
